analysis.one_liner: Bans nursing homes and home-care providers from forcing residents into pre-dispute arbitration agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let nursing home and home-care residents sue in court instead of being forced into private arbitration, never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would bar nursing homes and home-care providers serving Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries from requiring, accepting, or enforcing pre-dispute arbitration agreements — the fine-print contracts signed at admission that force families into private arbitration instead of court if a loved one is neglected or harmed. It would also wipe out existing arbitration agreements with residents and home-care clients. It was introduced by Rep. Linda Sánchez with 13 Democratic cosponsors, sent to two House committees, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid nursing home residents, people receiving Medicaid home- and community-based services, and home health care patients — along with their families. Anyone admitted to a nursing home would keep the right to take claims of neglect, abuse, or wrongful death to a court, where proceedings are public and damages are set by a judge or jury, rather than being steered into a private arbitration process chosen by the facility. Because the bill nullifies agreements already signed, current and former residents would regain court rights too.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nursing home and home-care patients and families

how_it_helps.text: Bars skilled nursing facilities and nursing homes serving Medicare and Medicaid residents from requiring, soliciting, accepting, or moving to enforce pre-dispute arbitration agreements with any resident — before, during, or after admission — and voids existing agreements so they cannot be enforced in court.

Extends the same ban to providers of Medicaid home- and community-based services and home health care, covering their employees, agents, and affiliates, so home-care clients get the same access to court as nursing home residents.

Requires that any dispute over whether the ban applies to an agreement be decided by a judge under federal law rather than by the arbitrator itself, closing the common loop where the arbitrator rules on its own authority.
Takes effect on the date of enactment, so residents and home-care clients already bound by arbitration agreements would regain their right to sue rather than waiting for new admissions.

analysis.who_pays: Nursing homes, nursing facility chains, and home-care providers, which would lose their most powerful legal shield: a signed arbitration agreement typically blocks residents from joining class actions or winning public jury verdicts for neglect or abuse, and arbitrators are selected through processes the industry controls. Arbitration providers would lose this stream of disputes. Facilities argue that defending cases in open court costs more, and some of that cost would be passed to residents or absorbed by an industry already operating on thin Medicaid margins.
analysis.who_pays_short: Nursing home and home-care provider companies

drawbacks.text: The ban is retroactive: it voids arbitration agreements already signed by current and former residents, which would unsettle contracts that were legal when signed and would likely draw court challenges over whether Congress can override the Federal Arbitration Act this way.

Litigation is generally slower and more expensive than arbitration, and nursing homes — many operating on tight Medicaid reimbursement margins — warn that open-court negligence suits add costs that can translate into higher prices for private-pay residents or facility closures in rural areas.

The bill covers only Medicare and Medicaid facilities and services, so providers serving purely private-pay clients could still use pre-dispute arbitration agreements, leaving an uneven rule across the sector.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and one-sided for residents: a signed arbitration clause at admission routinely means a family's only remedy for neglect or wrongful death is a confidential proceeding before an arbitrator chosen through a facility-controlled process, with no jury and no public record. The honest costs are that court cases cost facilities more, some of that is passed on to residents in an industry dependent on Medicaid rates, and the retroactive voiding of signed contracts invites legal fights. On balance, the bill traded modest, diffuse compliance costs for restoring a fundamental legal right to millions of vulnerable people; its main flaw is that Congress never seriously considered it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2024, sent to two House committees and then a health subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025 without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the Fairness in Nursing Home Arbitration Act on January 29, 2024, joined by 13 Democratic cosponsors.
The bill was referred to both the Ways and Means Committee and the Energy and Commerce Committee, splitting its jurisdiction, and was then sent to the Subcommittee on Health in February 2024.

The action record shows only a second referral to the Subcommittee on Health in December 2024 and no further action; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing home chains and home-care providers keep the arbitration agreements they have residents sign at admission, and the arbitration industry keeps the disputes those agreements channel away from courts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nursing home chains and arbitration providers

for.name: Rep. Linda T. Sánchez
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 13 cosponsors, all Democrats.

for.name: 13 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Schakowsky, Bonamici, Chu, DeGette, Doggett, Frost, Nadler, Norton, Pascrell, and Tonko.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was held before the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee took no action on the bill after referral; no hearing or markup was held before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican backed it; with Republicans chairing both committees of referral, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care facilities
industries.note: Facilities lose the arbitration agreements signed at admission that keep neglect and wrongful-death claims out of court, confidential, and before an arbitrator chosen through industry-controlled processes. Residents' interest in suing in court runs directly against the industry's interest in keeping those claims in arbitration.

industries.industry: Home care and home health providers
industries.note: Medicaid home- and community-based services and home health providers — and their employees and affiliates — would be barred from enforcing arbitration agreements against the clients they serve, exposing them to public lawsuits for harm to vulnerable people in their homes.

industries.industry: Arbitration and alternative dispute resolution firms
industries.note: These firms earn fees from resolving nursing home and home-care disputes privately; the bill wipes out that stream of pre-dispute cases and hands the disputes back to courts.
